full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I agree with the first pass on the clumping and I'm keeping its label. But I'd call the result plainly known, not a "variant", and I'd mark the type segregation as an artefact rather than a real finding.

**1. Clumping (nn_ratio = 0.3) is the documented behaviour of the Local Attraction Model.** What you describe is essentially Strömbom's Local Attraction Model (LAM): Daniel Strömbom. J Theor Biol. 2011. (vol. 283, pp. 145–151, doi:10.1016/j.jtbi.2011.05.019). In later work by the same group it is described as a self-propelled particle (SPP) model in which particles interact via local attraction alone and update their headings and positions synchronously. More specifically, on every time step t each particle calculates the position of the local center of mass (LCM) of other particles within a distance of R from it. One parameter controls how strongly agents steer toward that centre of mass, and depending on the relative strength of local attraction (c) groups of different type will be produced by the model. Your rule turns agents straight toward the centre of mass, with no memory of their previous heading. That puts it at the strong-attraction end of the LAM range, where agents form unpolarised swarms or tight clumps.

There is also a known reason why attraction alone gives very compact clusters: In order to avoid collapse of the particles to a point due to mutual attraction it is also often necessary to include a mutual repulsion between particles. Your rule has no repulsion, so dense clumps are the expected result. The clustering is real self-organisation, but it is a generic and well-understood outcome, close to a collapsed, nearly frozen state. Related background on noisy self-propelled particles held together by cohesion: We study the onset of collective motion, with and without cohesion, of groups of noisy self-propelled particles interacting locally. (Grégoire & Chaté, PRL 92, 025702, 2004). I also confirmed the "Refining self-propelled particle models" chapter (it is hosted on Erban's Oxford page). I did not check 2112.02974 or 1906.05542, and nothing here depends on them.

**2. "Type segregation" = 6.0 is almost certainly an artefact.** Types never enter the rule, and labels are assigned at random at the start. That means:
- Each cluster's type mix is just a random draw.
- Under a proper shuffle of the labels on the same positions, the expected excess of same-type neighbours is about zero. (Sampling without replacement even pushes it slightly negative.)
- No process exists that could sort agents by type.

A score of 6 most likely comes from one of these:
- a null model that randomises positions instead of labels;
- a baseline that doesn't account for clustering;
- chance variation when there are only a few, long-lasting clumps (roughly 400 agents split among maybe 10 frozen clusters).

I did not search for type sorting in this model, because nothing in a type-blind rule could produce it. The check that settles it is to shuffle labels within each snapshot and compare. I expect the signal to disappear.

**Searches run:** Strömbom's local-attraction model in J Theor Biol; cohesion-only noisy self-propelled particles / Grégoire–Chaté.
